summary:
El Salvador has no Gender Identity Law and no legal recognition of gender identity. A trans visitor carrying documents issued in another country has no domestic mechanism through which those documents could be aligned or challenged, and Salvadoran citizens face the same absence: in 2022 the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court ordered the Name Law reformed so that individuals could change their names to match their gender identity, holding the existing regime unconstitutional because it discriminated on the basis of gender, after a case brought by a transgender activist in 2016. As of 2023 the Legislative Assembly had enacted nothing, so transgender Salvadorans still cannot update official papers.

The penal code carries an enhanced penalty for bias-motivated killing. In September 2015 the National Assembly approved reforms under which homicides motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender draw 30 to 60 years under Article 129. The same 2015 reforms added sexual orientation and gender identity provisions to the Criminal Code carrying three to six years' imprisonment for discriminatory acts.

The limits of that framework are illustrated by the killing of Camila Díaz Córdova, a transgender Salvadoran woman deported from the United States, who was killed in January 2019. On 28 July 2020 a San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of her murder and sentenced each to 20 years. The judgment was the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for the killing of a transgender person; Human Rights Watch called it pivotal for transgender Salvadorans' rights, and advocates had argued during the prosecution that it could produce the country's first hate-crime homicide conviction.

Enforcement remains thin. About 500 hate crimes against LGBTQ people were reported between 1998 and 2015, with many more unattributed, and police have shown open refusal to cooperate in LGBT death investigations. Human Rights Watch reported in October 2020 that El Salvador, alongside Guatemala and Honduras, fails to address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people effectively, driving asylum claims abroad, and documented obstacles to obtaining protection in a full report issued in January 2021 with recommendations to the president, attorney general, congress and ministries. The peer-reviewed longitudinal dataset on killings of LGBTI+ people covering 2000 to 2020 was published by researchers at the Fundação Oswaldo Cruz in 2024.

Since the state of exception began in March 2022, trans women captured in mass raids have been held within the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. One woman arrested in San Salvador on 14 April 2022 was held first in police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out with another trans woman for punishment drills in the sun while handcuffed and forced to squat, and denied her access to an HIV clinic. A judge released her after about four months, finding the arrest unsupported; the other woman remained imprisoned. Human-rights organisations attribute the abuse directly to the absence of a Gender Identity Law, and trans detainees are placed by birth sex in the general prison population.

Prison conditions are explicitly hostile to gender nonconformity. Homosexual inmates are forbidden from dressing or behaving in an effeminate manner, and gender-nonconforming men are targeted by police officers, soldiers and prison guards through unwarranted searches, theft of property, sexual assault and other physical violence. In a 1999 investigation, two transvestite detainees were forced to wear men's clothing for their hearing.

Healthcare access carries its own risks. Hospital specialists frequently dismiss trans patients' complaints as a side effect of being transgender, and patients are sometimes made to wait longer or refused care, a pattern that can be applied discreetly. There are no protocols or programmes for hormone therapy or sex reassignment surgery, and studies record that many trans women avoid seeking medical help after surgical complications because they have learned not to trust the system. Psychological care, where LGBT people obtain it, often takes the form of conversion therapies. Against this, the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance issued guidelines in April 2009 banning discrimination against LGBT and HIV-positive people in health services, and a 2009 national HIV/AIDS plan prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in healthcare.

Violence risk is reinforced by public attitudes. A 2013 study found that 62% of Salvadorans do not accept homosexuality and 85% believe it acceptable to attack a transgender individual on the basis of their identity. Gang violence includes targeting of LGBT people through physical and sexual assault, forced recruitment and extortion for protection, and police cooperation in investigating such attacks is unreliable.

There is no recognition of same-sex partnerships. Article 11 of the Family Code defines marriage as a heterosexual union, same-sex couples may not adopt as a couple, and the Law on Family Violence does not apply to same-sex couples. Since 2006 there have been proposals to amend the Constitution to bar recognition even of same-sex couples married abroad. Two challenges to the marriage ban were dismissed on technical and procedural grounds, on 20 December 2016 and 17 January 2019, although the Constitutional Court declared a proposed marriage ban unlawful in January 2018 and admitted a recognition lawsuit for hearing in August 2019 following the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of January 2018.
tangentialFactors:
El Salvador's record is discussed together with Guatemala and Honduras, where Human Rights Watch found the same failure to address anti-LGBT violence, and the resulting displacement has produced a steady stream of asylum claims in the United States. Camila Díaz Córdova herself had been deported from the United States shortly before her killing.

Organised religion and machismo shape the environment. Over half the population identifies as actively practising Catholic and much of the remainder attends evangelical churches, whose leaders have organised opposition to LGBT rights legislation. A documented cultural expectation equates Salvadoran identity with virility, and being described as gay carries social cost for heterosexual men.

Public opinion on legal recognition of same-sex relationships has remained low: a 2010 poll recorded 10% support and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 19%. The 2013 study recording 85% acceptance of violence against transgender individuals places El Salvador among the most socially hostile countries in its region.

Conversion therapy is commonly applied within families, including to children, with expulsion from the home and severance of contact where it fails. LGBT students whose gender expression does not match the sex assigned at birth drop out of school at high rates and some have been expelled outright; sexuality is absent from the school curriculum, which pushes LGBT students into invisibility.

Gay and bisexual men are permitted to donate blood, with policy excluding those who engage in what authorities classify as risky behaviour. San Salvador authorised permanent rainbow paintings at several crossroads in July 2017, and the country's first Gay Pride parade was held in June 1997 to commemorate a massacre of trans women in the 1980s.
localsOnly:
Transgender Salvadorans cannot change the gender or name on official documents: the Constitutional Chamber's 2022 order to reform the Name Law has not been implemented, and the Legislative Assembly had taken no action as of 2023.

An Institutional Policy for the Care of the LGBT Population, adopted in 2018, allows LGBT people to file legal complaints against discrimination, and the Ministry of Public Health's April 2009 guidelines prohibit discrimination against LGBT and HIV-positive people in health services. Neither instrument has produced reliable protection in practice, and the Law on Family Violence does not extend to same-sex couples.

Residents live with the practical consequences of birth-sex placement in the ordinary prison system: no special custody provision exists for trans detainees, and gender-nonconforming inmates are punished for dress and manner. Housing and family exclusion are common routes out of the home for LGBT young people, and mental-health support is frequently delivered as conversion therapy.

Since March 2022 the state of exception has exposed trans women to arbitrary arrest, placement in police lockups and prisons without gender-identity accommodation, denial of clinic access and punitive treatment by custodians, with release depending on a judge finding the arrest unsupported.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state whether the Article 129 enhanced range of 30 to 60 years was charged or applied in the Camila Díaz Córdova case; the three police officers were sentenced to 20 years each on 28 July 2020. Whether that conviction has produced further hate-crime prosecutions against trans victims is not sourced.

Status of the Name Law reform ordered in 2022 is sourced only up to 2023, when the Legislative Assembly had acted nothing. Later legislative or judicial developments are unresolved in this inventory.

The outcome for the second trans woman detained alongside the released petitioner, identified as Rosa, is unresolved as of the February 2024 reporting; no subsequent judgment is sourced.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules, airport or border document screening, or how a foreign passport's gender marker is treated on arrival. That layer remains not sourced here.

No source documents discrimination by private businesses, accommodation providers or transport operators against trans visitors, nor the practical availability of the 2018 complaint mechanism to a foreign national.
